title: The Presidents of Prices: Corso Novara, Eighty Days, and the Widow's Answer
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Palma Campania, a son to a carter
stops.date_confidence: attested; date and town agree in both the English and Italian entries
stops.campa: A son is born on the twenty-sixth of February 1926 to a carter and a housewife in Palma Campania, a Vesuvian market town that lives off the produce roads into Naples. The father hauls other men's goods; the family owns none of the land the crates come from. No source names the street or the house. The name the boy will carry is not this town's: Pascalone 'e Nola, big Pasquale from Nola, after the market seven kilometres north-northwest where he will make his money. He will be married in this town in April 1955.
suggested_refs: Civil birth registers of the comune of Palma Campania, province of Naples, 1926
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pasquale Simonetti' (English)
Wikipedia, 'Pasquale Simonetti' (Italian)
OpenStreetMap relation 40807, Palma Campania comune boundary

stops.name: Palma Campania, the years nobody wrote down
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; no source records any incident of his childhood, and this date is a placeholder inside the blank
stops.campa: Between the birth register and the war the record is empty. No school, no incident, no first job, no first arrest: nothing of his boyhood is written down anywhere reachable. What the town offered a poor child born in 1926 is cart wheels, produce crates, and the mountain at the edge of vision. His father moves other people's property for a fee, standing between the peasants who grow the food and the men who will later price it. In 1935 the boy is nine years old.
suggested_refs: Parish and school records of Palma Campania for the 1930s, not located in this research
sources: Reconstruction from the father's attested trade (Wikipedia, 'Pasquale Simonetti', English) and regional context; no direct childhood source found

stops.name: Naples, the falsified ration books
stops.date_confidence: year not attested; no source dates the racket within the war, and 1943 is a placement, not a record
stops.campa: Under the Allied occupation Naples runs on scarcity, and scarcity has its own currency. Simonetti forges ration books and sells them on the black market: paper before produce, need before price. What he does at Corso Novara a decade later is this same trade at scale, in daylight, with a sack of potatoes standing in for a loaf of bread. No source consulted gives a year within the war, and the year carried here is a placement rather than a record. None names a street, and none names an accomplice.
suggested_refs: Allied Military Government ration-control files for the province of Naples, 1943-1945
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pasquale Simonetti' (English): 'falsifying ration books for food which he then sold on the black market'

stops.name: Naples, from paper to cigarettes
stops.date_confidence: not attested; the late-1940s placement is the researcher's, since no source dates his entry into the contraband trade
stops.campa: After the war the trade turns to cigarettes, brought in by sea and moved inland by men who fight each other for the routes. Four ports feed the traffic, named together in a single sentence of the record: Marseille, Gibraltar, Nice, Tangiers. Rival gangs compete violently for control, and Simonetti is one of the competitors. What the smuggling teaches him is that the money sits in the permission to move goods rather than in the goods themselves. He is twenty-two.
suggested_refs: Guardia di Finanza contraband seizure records, port of Naples, late 1940s
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pasquale Simonetti' (English), naming Marseille, Gibraltar, Nice and Tangiers and the violent competition for the routes

stops.name: Marseille, a port of the trade
stops.date_confidence: no date and no visit attested; the port is named as a node of the traffic, nothing more
stops.campa: Marseille stands at the head of the contraband chain that feeds Naples, the first of four ports named in the record of Simonetti's cigarette years. The record gives the port and nothing else about it: no ship, no cargo weight, no crossing. Nothing places him on this quay. The tobacco comes down through the western Mediterranean in other men's holds and reaches him at the far end, in the streets behind the Naples station, where it is broken up and sold.
suggested_refs: French customs records for tobacco transhipment through Marseille, late 1940s
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pasquale Simonetti' (English), which names the four ports as sources of the traffic and does not place Simonetti at any of them

stops.name: Gibraltar, a port of the trade
stops.date_confidence: no date and no visit attested; the port is named as a node of the traffic, nothing more
stops.campa: Gibraltar is the second of the four, a British rock at the mouth of the sea where duty-free tobacco can be loaded legally and landed illegally eight hundred miles away. Simonetti is not recorded here either. The Naples end of the chain is what the sources describe: gangs competing violently for control of routes that run to places most of the men fighting over them will never see. No Italian source consulted names Gibraltar. The English one names it once, in a list of four.
suggested_refs: Gibraltar tobacco re-export licences and Italian contraband prosecutions of the same years
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pasquale Simonetti' (English)

stops.name: Nice, a port of the trade
stops.date_confidence: no date and no visit attested; the port is named as a node of the traffic, nothing more
stops.campa: Nice is the third port named, a short run along the coast from the Italian border and a natural transhipment point for goods meant to arrive in Campania without arriving through customs. There is no attested visit. What mattered was that the cigarettes came, not that any particular man went. Simonetti's authority is exercised at the receiving end, where the crates are divided and the shares fixed. The record gives four port names in one sentence and no itinerary at all.
suggested_refs: Franco-Italian border customs seizures, Alpes-Maritimes, late 1940s
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pasquale Simonetti' (English)

stops.name: Tangier, a port of the trade
stops.date_confidence: no date and no visit attested; the port is named as a node of the traffic, nothing more
stops.campa: Tangier, then an international zone with its own rules, closes the western arc: Marseille, Gibraltar, Nice, Tangiers, four names for the water between North Africa and Provence, all of it emptying into Naples. Whether Simonetti ever crossed to any of them is not stated in any of the sources consulted here, and no crossing is supplied to fill the silence. He is documented in Campania, at the point where the trade turns into cash, and nowhere west of it.
suggested_refs: Tangier International Zone shipping registers, 1946-1952
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pasquale Simonetti' (English)

stops.name: Corso Novara, the market taken
stops.date_confidence: year attested only as approximate; no month or day is given in any source
stops.campa: By 1950 the fruit and vegetable exchange at Corso Novara, by the rail line into Napoli Centrale, is his. Campania sends thirty percent of Italy's produce, and men like Simonetti are called the presidents of prices: they fix what a crate costs before it reaches a shop and take a cut for the fixing. On the potato transactions alone the price president earns three or four million lire a day. Farmers who decline the arrangement are told what declining costs. Antonio Esposito holds the title beside him.
suggested_refs: The wholesale produce exchange of Corso Novara, Rione Vasto, Naples
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pasquale Simonetti' (English)
TerraNostraNews.it, 'Gomorra dalla A alla Z, i guappi del secondo dopoguerra' (2016)
OpenStreetMap way 326263990, Corso Novara

stops.name: Naples, the size of the man
stops.date_confidence: undated; the description is not tied to any occasion or year in the source
stops.campa: A contemporary, quoted in the scholarly literature, describes him: a tall man, close to two metres, gigantic, carrying himself in the guappo manner and self-assured with it. The size is where half the name comes from. Pascalone is the augmentative of Pasquale, big Pasquale, given for his bulk; 'e Nola is where he works, not where he was born. Who said it is not recorded. The phrase reaches print through Percy Allum's study of postwar Naples, quoting an informant the study does not name.
stops.quote: He was a tall man, nearly two meters, a gigantic man who always had a way of behaving, a 'guappaesica' way of doing things, a self-assured man
suggested_refs: Percy Allum, Politics and Society in Post-War Naples, p. 370
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pasquale Simonetti' (English), citing Allum 2000, p. 370
Wikipedia, 'Assunta Maresca' (Italian), for the nickname given 'per la sua mole'

stops.name: Nola, a hundred lire the quintal
stops.date_confidence: undated in the source; placed inside the early-1950s presidency
stops.campa: At the Nola market he takes a hundred lire on every quintal of potatoes sold. A small levy, repeated at the scale of a region's staple crop, on a trade nobody in Campania can go around: the arithmetic is the whole arrangement. How many quintals crossed the scales in a day is recorded nowhere consulted, and the figure sometimes quoted is a back-calculation from his daily earnings rather than a reported number. The hundred lire come off the top, before the grower is paid.
suggested_refs: The wholesale potato market of Nola, province of Naples
sources: TerraNostraNews.it, 'Gomorra dalla A alla Z, i guappi del secondo dopoguerra' (2016), for the 100 lire per quintal

stops.name: Pomigliano d'Arco, the partner's name
stops.date_confidence: undated; the partnership is described in the sources without dates
stops.campa: Antonio Esposito carries this town in his name, Totonno 'e Pomigliano, and for a stretch of the early 1950s he and Simonetti are partners rather than enemies, dividing the chain that runs from harvest to price to distribution. He deals in dried fruit and nuts and keeps company with politicians. Partnership between price presidents does not last: there is only so much toll, and two men are dividing it. When Esposito is buried, twelve deputies are said to have sent wreaths, and the chronicle that reports it says only that this was said.
suggested_refs: TerraNostraNews.it on Antonio Esposito, dried-fruit producer and market boss
sources: TerraNostraNews.it, 'Gomorra dalla A alla Z' (2016): 'produttore di frutta secca e in buoni rapporti con i politici, tanto che al suo funerale si disse che ben dodici deputati inviarono corone di fiori'

stops.name: Scafati, a town in the network
stops.date_confidence: undated; the town is named as part of the network, without a dated incident
stops.campa: Scafati lies inside the produce belt the price-fixing reaches, one of the towns named alongside Pomigliano, Pagani and Marano as part of the trading network the postwar bosses carved between them. No incident ties Simonetti to Scafati by name, and the chronicle gives the town one mention and no episode. Its crates go north out of the Sarno plain to be counted and priced at Nola and at Corso Novara, by men who never come here to see what they are pricing.
suggested_refs: The agricultural markets of the Sarno plain, Scafati and its neighbours
sources: TerraNostraNews.it, 'Gomorra dalla A alla Z' (2016), naming Scafati among the network towns; no Simonetti incident attached

stops.name: Pagani, a town in the network
stops.date_confidence: undated; the town is named as part of the network, without a dated incident
stops.campa: Pagani sits further down the plain toward Salerno, named in the same account as part of the network under the produce bosses' control. The fruit that leaves here is the fruit taxed at Nola and sold at Corso Novara; the region works as one market with many gates. Where one boss's zone ended and another's began was drawn on no surviving map, and was probably never drawn anywhere except in the understanding between the men themselves. No episode and no date attach to Pagani.
suggested_refs: The produce markets of the Agro Nocerino-Sarnese
sources: TerraNostraNews.it, 'Gomorra dalla A alla Z' (2016), naming Pagani among the network towns; no Simonetti incident attached

stops.name: Marano di Napoli, the ally's ground
stops.date_confidence: undated; Baiano's association with Marano is stated without a date
stops.campa: Marano is Raffaele Baiano's town, and Baiano stands with Simonetti when the shooting starts. It is allied ground rather than a frontier, whatever later accounts have made of it: north of the city, in the belt of contraband and produce, a place his side of the arrangement holds. The Nuvoletta family will become dominant here afterward, in a Camorra that no longer resembles the market presidencies of the early fifties. Nothing in the record puts Simonetti himself in these streets.
suggested_refs: TerraNostraNews.it on Raffaele Baiano of Marano and the later Nuvoletta ascendancy
sources: TerraNostraNews.it, 'Gomorra dalla A alla Z' (2016), which names Marano as Baiano's home town and not as Maisto's territory

stops.name: Giugliano in Campania, the rival's ground
stops.date_confidence: undated for the rivalry; the 1971 arrest and the death at fifty-eight are attested separately
stops.campa: West of the city, Alfredo Maisto runs Giugliano the way Simonetti runs Corso Novara, as a territory with a price list. Maisto's family holds a mill and land here; Simonetti has no ancestral claim to anything, only a market he has taken. Born in Giugliano in 1918, Maisto will be arrested in Rome in 1971 over the 1967 killing of Domenico Mallardo, and will die in a clinic at fifty-eight of a thrombosis. Whether he was acquitted is not in the source; it records the accusation and stops.
suggested_refs: TerraNostraNews.it on Alfredo Maisto of Giugliano and the Mallardo case
sources: TerraNostraNews.it, 'Gomorra dalla A alla Z' (2016): 'Nel 1971 Alfredo Maisto viene arrestato a Roma'; 'muore in clinica a soli 58 anni per una trombosi'

stops.name: Naples, flowers for a wedding or a funeral
stops.date_confidence: undated anecdote; no source places it in a year
stops.campa: Enforcement, in his hands, is not always a gun. A young man who has left a pregnant girlfriend is put a question: whether he would rather spend ten thousand lire on flowers for his wedding or for his funeral. The sources offer it as evidence of method, a man policing the district's morals along with its prices. It reaches print through Percy Allum's study and through a memorial site kept in Simonetti's name, always as reported speech. Nobody transcribed the line at the time.
suggested_refs: Percy Allum, Politics and Society in Post-War Naples, pp. 142-45
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pasquale Simonetti' (English): 'Simonetti asked the young man, if he preferred spending ten thousand lire in flowers on his marriage or his funeral', citing Allum 2000, pp. 142-45, and tinosimonetti.it

stops.name: Naples, the slap he is said to have given
stops.date_confidence: undated anecdote, flagged as such by the source itself; the year here is arbitrary
stops.campa: One story, carried by a book called Il guappo and repeated since without corroboration, has Simonetti slapping Lucky Luciano somewhere in this city, the American boss deported to Italy and living out his last years in Naples. No restaurant is named, no street, no date, no witness. It survives because it is the shape a city likes: its own hardest man measured against the most famous gangster it can produce. The source that carries it calls it anecdote, and it is repeated here as anecdote. Whether the two men were ever in a room together is a question the record does not answer.
suggested_refs: The book Il guappo, cited by the Italian entry for the Luciano episode; not consulted in this research
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pasquale Simonetti' (Italian), citing the book 'Il guappo'; flagged in the source as an undated anecdote

stops.name: Melito di Napoli, pistols in the streets
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no month or day given in any source
stops.campa: The two groups meet with pistols in the streets of Melito di Napoli. Simonetti has Raffaele Baiano with him; the other side is Alfredo Maisto's. The fight is over market territory, which in this trade means over who sets the price at which a district's produce moves. What the casualties were, and whose they were, does not come down in the sources reachable here. The chronicle that records it names the town and nothing finer: nelle strade di Melito.
suggested_refs: Court of Naples proceedings arising from the 1952 Melito shoot-out
sources: TerraNostraNews.it, 'Gomorra dalla A alla Z' (2016): 'I due gruppi si affrontarono a colpi di pistola nelle strade di Melito'
Wikipedia, 'Pasquale Simonetti' (English), for the resulting charge

stops.name: Naples, eight years and three months
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no month or day given, and no court or archival citation was located
stops.campa: For the Melito shooting he is tried and convicted of attempted murder: eight years and three months. He is twenty-seven. The year is 1953, and no source consulted gives the month, the courtroom, the judge, or an archival reference for the judgment. What became of Raffaele Baiano, who fought the same fight on the same side, is not recorded either. The market goes on without him. Antonio Esposito sits in the booth and collects the same toll on the same crates, and the growers pay it to a different name.
suggested_refs: The 1953 attempted-murder judgment against Simonetti, no archival reference located
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pasquale Simonetti' (English)

stops.name: Poggioreale, the years with nothing in them
stops.date_confidence: facility inferred, not attested: no source consulted names the prison that held him
stops.campa: Poggioreale is where a Naples sentence is served, and Poggioreale is where he is presumed to be, though no source consulted names the prison. The sentence on paper is eight years and three months. Two years pass. Outside, the presidency of prices continues under other hands and the arrangement he built proves indifferent to his absence. Inside, nothing at all is recorded of him: no visit, no letter, no incident. He goes in at twenty-six and comes out at twenty-eight.
suggested_refs: Detention registers of the Casa Circondariale di Napoli Poggioreale, 1953-1954
sources: Inference from Wikipedia, 'Pasquale Simonetti' (English), which gives the sentence and the release but names no facility

stops.name: Poggioreale, out at Christmas
stops.date_confidence: attested as Christmas 1954; the exact day is the holiday itself, not a documented release date
stops.campa: He walks out at Christmas 1954, having served roughly two years of a sentence of eight years and three months. On paper it still has six years to run. No pardon and no amnesty is named in the sources; nothing explains the release beyond whatever the ordinary mechanics of an Italian sentence allow. Where he goes first, and who meets him, is not recorded. He is twenty-eight. Four months later he will be married. Eighty days after that he will be dead.
suggested_refs: Release records for the 1953 sentence, not located in this research
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pasquale Simonetti' (English): 'At Christmas 1954, Simonetti left prison, after serving two years of his sentence'

stops.name: Corso Novara, the market he comes back to
stops.date_confidence: undated; no source records a date, a meeting, or a quarrel between the two men after the release
stops.campa: He comes back to a market that has learned to run without him. Esposito held the business through the two years and, by the account carried in the sources, did not keep the share he had promised. There is no document of a confrontation, no dated quarrel, no recorded word between them. Everything between the release and the killing is inference from the outcome, and the outcome is this: within seven months, one of the two partners commissions the killing of the other.
suggested_refs: The Corso Novara wholesale exchange under Esposito's control, 1953-1955
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pupetta Maresca' (English), for Esposito's takeover and the withheld share

stops.name: Castellammare di Stabia, the engagement
stops.date_confidence: the courtship is placed between the December 1954 release and the April 1955 wedding; no source dates it
stops.campa: Assunta Maresca, called Pupetta, was born in this port town on the gulf on 19 January 1935, into a family already inside the Camorra: her father is a boss in his own right. Simonetti courts her after his release and they are engaged within months. She is twenty. He is twenty-nine, out of prison a matter of weeks, and a name in every produce market between here and Nola. Some later accounts make her barely eighteen at the wedding; the dates do not support them.
suggested_refs: Civil registers of Castellammare di Stabia, birth of Assunta Maresca, 19 January 1935
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pupetta Maresca' (English)
Wikipedia, 'Assunta Maresca' (Italian)

stops.name: Palma Campania, five hundred guests
stops.date_confidence: attested; date and venue confirmed, the venue against a Naples variant carried elsewhere
stops.campa: On 27 April 1955 he marries Assunta Maresca in his birthplace, before more than five hundred guests, and the whole town turns out to wish them well. The man who will order the groom's death in eighty days signs the register: Antonio Esposito, the partner from Pomigliano, stands as a witness to the marriage. She is twenty years and three months old and already pregnant; how far along is not stated in either entry. Whether Alfredo Maisto is also in the room is repeated in some accounts and confirmed by none.
suggested_refs: Marriage register of Palma Campania, 27 April 1955
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pasquale Simonetti' (English): 'The whole town of Palma Campania turned out to wish them well'
Wikipedia, 'Assunta Maresca' (Italian): 'Testimone di nozze fu Antonio Esposito'

stops.name: Corso Novara, the shooting in the market
stops.date_confidence: contradiction: 16 July per the English entry and the Italian entry on Simonetti, 15 July per the Italian entry on Maresca; unresolved
stops.campa: Eighty days after the wedding, Carlo Gaetano Orlando, called Tanino 'e Bastimento, shoots him at Corso Novara in the middle of a working market, on Antonio Esposito's commission. The English entry names a second gunman, Gaetano Nuvoletta, who appears in no Italian source consulted. One chronicle gives the killer a line before he fires, and gives the pretext as a slight almost too small to translate: a greeting not returned. The Italian entry on his widow dates the killing to the fifteenth instead.
stops.quote_source: TerraNostraNews.it, 'Gomorra dalla A alla Z, i guappi del secondo dopoguerra' (2016), attributed to the killer at the moment of the shooting
suggested_refs: The Corso Novara market place, Rione Vasto, scene of the killing of 16 July 1955
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pasquale Simonetti' (English): 'in the Corso Novara, the busy market place of Naples'
Wikipedia, 'Assunta Maresca' (Italian), which gives 15 July
TerraNostraNews.it (2016)

stops.name: Ospedale degli Incurabili, two versions of an hour
stops.date_confidence: contested: the sources reviewed here name no hospital at all, while a separate account gives the Incurabili and death from peritonitis on 16 or 17 July
stops.campa: What happens in the minutes after the shots is not recorded. The sources reviewed here name no hospital, no ambulance, no doctor: broad daylight, a public market, a body, and then nothing until the funeral. A separate account in circulation carries him to the Ospedale degli Incurabili, which has taken in the wounded of Naples since the sixteenth century, and has him die there of peritonitis. Nothing consulted decides between the two. Did he reach a bed alive at all?
suggested_refs: Admission and mortuary registers of the Ospedale degli Incurabili, Naples, July 1955
sources: Absence noted in Wikipedia (English and Italian) and TerraNostraNews.it accounts
The Incurabili and peritonitis version, carried in circulation and not corroborated in the sources reviewed here

stops.name: Palma Campania, the grave nobody names
stops.date_confidence: burial date and place both unattested; placed immediately after the killing as a likelihood, not a record
stops.campa: No source consulted names his grave. It is reasonable, and no more than reasonable, that a man born and married out of Palma Campania was buried from it too, among the family that raised him. Who came to the funeral, who stayed away out of guilt or fear, what was said over him, whether a stone was cut and where it stands: none of it survives in anything reachable. No monument, street name, or civic marker to him was found in either Palma Campania or Nola. His widow, three months pregnant and eighty days married, appears in no account of the burial.
suggested_refs: Cemetery registers of Palma Campania and Nola, July 1955, not located in this research
sources: Gap: no burial record found in any source consulted
Wikipedia, 'Nola' (Italian), whose notable-figures section does not mention Simonetti

stops.name: Naples, what she decides
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; no source dates a decision, and the motive itself is tradition rather than testimony
stops.campa: In the weeks after the killing his widow reaches the conclusion the whole story turns on: that the police know who ordered it and will not act. The motive is repeated in the popular literature and appears in neither Wikipedia entry as retrieved, so it is carried here as tradition and not as testimony. No source dates the decision, and none records who, if anyone, she told. She is twenty, pregnant, and widowed eighty days into a marriage five hundred people attended.
suggested_refs: Maresca's own later statements on her motive, in interviews not located in this research
sources: Reconstruction; the stated motive was not found in Wikipedia, 'Pupetta Maresca' (English) or 'Assunta Maresca' (Italian) as retrieved

stops.name: Naples, the fourth of October
stops.date_confidence: contradiction: 4 October per both Italian entries, 4 August per the English entry, 16 September per a third source; October is the only date consistent with the arrest ten days later
stops.campa: On 4 October 1955 she finds Antonio Esposito and kills him. Both Italian entries give that date; the English entry gives 4 August, a fourth account gives 16 September, and October is the only one that fits an arrest ten days later. She is in her sixth month. The English entry has her firing twenty-nine shots from a Smith and Wesson .38 held in both hands, and explains why she used both. The Italian entry reports investigators who counted at least four pistols. No source names the street.
stops.quote: I was afraid I would miss
stops.quote_source: Wikipedia, 'Pupetta Maresca' (English), her explanation for holding the revolver in both hands
suggested_refs: The investigation file into the killing of Antonio Esposito, Naples, October 1955
sources: Wikipedia, 'Assunta Maresca' (Italian): 'il 4 ottobre, Assunta - al sesto mese di gravidanza - uccise il presunto mandante dell'omicidio: Antonio Esposito'; 'i colpi partirono da almeno quattro pistole'
Wikipedia, 'Pupetta Maresca' (English), which gives 4 August and 29 shots
Italiamistero.it, which gives 16 September

stops.name: Naples, the arrest ten days later
stops.date_confidence: attested; the date is undisputed across sources
stops.campa: She is arrested on 14 October 1955, ten days after the killing of Antonio Esposito, in Naples. She has not left the region. There is no account of hiding, no attempt at a border, nothing in the record that looks like flight. For ten days she stays in a city where everyone knows what has happened and who did it. She is in her sixth month. No source names the place of the arrest or the officers who made it. Four years later she will tell a courtroom that she would do it again.
suggested_refs: Arrest and committal records, Naples, 14 October 1955
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pupetta Maresca' (English)
Wikipedia, 'Assunta Maresca' (Italian)

stops.name: Poggioreale, the son born inside
stops.date_confidence: year retained from the sources; no date is given by either entry, and January is derived from a sixth month of pregnancy in October 1955
stops.campa: The prison presumed to have held her husband holds her, and here their son is born. He is named Pasquale for his father and called Pasqualino, and he arrives into a cell rather than a household, in the year after a killing his mother answered with another killing. He will not live past eighteen. What the birth was like, and who attended it, is nowhere described. Neither entry gives a date: the English says only in prison, the Italian only nel corso della sua detenzione.
suggested_refs: Prison birth records, Naples, 1956, not located in this research
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pupetta Maresca' (English): born 'in prison'
Wikipedia, 'Assunta Maresca' (Italian): 'nel corso della sua detenzione'

stops.name: Castel Capuano, the court and the answer
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested; the exact day is not given, and the courthouse building is a likely placement rather than a confirmed one
stops.campa: Her trial opens before the Naples Court of Assizes in April 1959, nearly four years after the shooting, and draws the international press. She tells the court she would do it again, and the room, by the account that comes down, bursts into cheers. Eighteen years, reduced on appeal to thirteen years and four months. That the court sat in Castel Capuano, the Norman castle the city has used as its hall of justice for four centuries, is likely rather than separately confirmed in the sources consulted.
stops.quote_source: Wikipedia, 'Pupetta Maresca' (English), reporting her testimony at the April 1959 trial
suggested_refs: Castel Capuano, seat of the Naples courts, and the Assizes file of April 1959
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pupetta Maresca' (English)

stops.name: Naples, Rosi films La sfida
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no release month established in this research
stops.campa: Three years after the killing Francesco Rosi shoots his first feature in the same market world it describes, freely inspired by the deaths of Simonetti and Esposito. The dead man becomes Vito Polara; the wife keeps the name Assunta. The produce boss shot at Corso Novara has been dead thirty-eight months and is already a character, played by an actor, in cinemas in the city where he was killed. It takes the Silver Lion at Venice in 1958 and three Nastri d'argento the year after.
suggested_refs: Francesco Rosi, La sfida (1958), with Rosanna Schiaffino and Jose Suarez
sources: Wikipedia, 'La sfida (film)' (Italian): 'liberamente ispirato'; Leone d'argento, Venice 1958; three Nastri d'argento, 1959

stops.name: Naples, Pasqualino does not come home
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no month or day given by either entry
stops.campa: In 1974 the son born in prison disappears at eighteen. The English entry says he was abducted and murdered; the Italian says only that he vanished, in an ambush, and that the body was never found. He had opposed his mother's relationship with the camorrista Umberto Ammaturo, and she suspected Ammaturo of his death. His father was shot in a market in daylight in front of witnesses, nineteen years earlier. For the second Pasquale Simonetti there is no body and no verdict.
suggested_refs: Missing-person and homicide files for Pasquale Simonetti junior, Naples, 1974
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pupetta Maresca' (English): 'abducted and murdered at the age of 18'
Wikipedia, 'Pasquale Simonetti' (Italian): 'scomparve', body never found

stops.name: Naples, the story on Canale 5
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the broadcast was delayed by controversy and no firm transmission date is established here
stops.campa: Fifty-eight years after the killing a television miniseries puts the story on Canale 5, with Manuela Arcuri as Pupetta. Simonetti is refracted into a character called Michele De Nicola, the nipote of a murdered fruit vendor, an Italian word that will not settle between nephew and grandson; Massimiliano Morra plays him, and he dies in her arms, killed on the orders of a rival boss. Assunta Maresca consulted on the set. Afterward she said her life had been distorted. She was seventy-eight.
suggested_refs: Pupetta - Il coraggio e la passione, Canale 5, 2013
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pupetta - Il coraggio e la passione' (Italian): Arcuri as Pupetta, Morra as Michele De Nicola, killed on the orders of Don Luigi Vitiello; Maresca as on-set consultant and her later objection; the delayed broadcast

stops.name: Naples, what the city keeps
stops.date_confidence: not an event; undated and continuing popular memory, placed last in the sequence for want of a date
stops.campa: The story does not stay with the two people at its center, or in the decade that produced it. It becomes a sceneggiata plot, retold in songs and films and finally on television, the market killing and the pregnant widow's answer working as civic legend long after the produce presidents are forgotten by name. What gets remembered is her, standing up in a courtroom. What she was answering for, a man and a market and a toll of a hundred lire the quintal, is remembered less.
suggested_refs: The sceneggiata tradition of Naples and its treatments of the Simonetti-Maresca story
